dossier.public_summary: The dip changes depth far more than expected between sectors and even within the same data product, and the few individual transits are not consistent — one is missing and one is twice as deep. The Gaia astrometry also shows high scatter suggesting the star is disturbed. Together this looks like a variable or blended binary or systematic noise near the target, not a stable 3.4-Earth-radius planet.

reasons.why: Depth changes dramatically between sectors and within the QLP source itself, not a calibration offset. Expected aperture dependence for a blended neighbour, not a planet on the target.
reasons.value: p_constant=0.001538, depth_change_pct=114.6, verdict=changes_within_a_source, per-sector 2941±2767 ppm (S35), 9486±1012 ppm (S62), 4702±1051 ppm (S89)

reasons.why: Single-transit depths are wildly inconsistent; one transit is basically missing and one is ~2x deeper, driving ~88% of the signal. Points to a few bad/systematic events, not repeatable planet transits.

reasons.why: Marginally significant odd/even difference plus very high astrometric excess noise indicates a binary/variability/blend scenario. Combined with depth scatter, an EB or NEB on a neighbour better explains the signal than a stable planet. A main-sequence EB can be flat-bottomed with no secondary, so flat shape alone does not favour planet.

reasons.why: Difference imaging cannot place the dip on target; it is consistent with the target but also with several neighbours that could fake it, so centroid does not reject an off-target EB. No positive planet signature survives.
